extracted.intended_audience: architects, patrons, artists, craftsmen, and church authorities involved in designing or funding ecclesiastical and civic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles for designing, funding, and executing ornament and workmanship in ecclesiastical (and civic) architecture, emphasizing sacrifice, honesty of materials/workmanship, appropriate distribution of ornament, and the moral priorities of ministry versus display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costliness of offering
rubrics_metrics.description: That costliness was _generally_ a condition of the acceptableness of the sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that offerings must in some degree cost the giver to be acceptable; sacrificial costliness testifies respect and devotion (scriptural citations: 2 Sam. xxiv.24; Deut. xvi.16-17). This applies to gifts toward churches and to the sacrifice of skill/time by craftsmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer the best of their kind
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition of their acceptableness will be now, as it was then, that they should be the best of their kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The offering should be the best quality available—not because lesser things fail typologically, but because offering inferior things indicates a grudging spirit and dishonours God. Patrons and builders should present the best workmanship/materials they can afford; poorer but honest work is preferable to bad attempts at high art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and splendor as memorial of covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptance of that covenant might be marked and signified by use, in some external sign of their love and obedience, and that their gratitude... might have at once their expression and their enduring testimony in the presentation to Him... of all treasures of wisdom and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art, beauty and skill in sacred buildings are legitimate as external signs and memorials of devotion: thought and labor, wood and stone, iron and gold should be offered. This frames decoration as an act of remembrance and gratitude rather than mere display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of ministry over decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: A better and more honorable offering is made to our Master in ministry to the poor... than in material presents to His temple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If practical needs (places to pray, roofs/walls, teaching, daily bread) are unmet, they take precedence over adornment. Architects, patrons and church authorities must not sacrifice essential ministry or welfare for superficial decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer private luxuries to sacred service
rubrics_metrics.description: The tesselated colors on our floors... are, or they ought to be, the signs that enough has been devoted to the great purposes of human stewardship, and that there remains to us what we can spend in luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private domestic extravagances should not be kept while the church remains bare; a portion of private luxury ought to be offered to sacred service. Ruskin gives the practical exhortation that modest sacrifice of domestic vanities could fund substantial church building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid meaningless domestic vanities
rubrics_metrics.description: Things which have become foolishly and apathetically habitual... cornicings of ceilings and graining of doors... things which cause half the expense of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between true magnificence and pointless, habitual finery. Avoid spending on unnoticed or functionless ornament—redirect such expenditure toward meaningful public/sacred works. The author permits genuine beauty in private houses but condemns useless expense that destroys comfort and honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devote best labor and expenditure to sacred art
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts will never flourish until they have been primarily devoted to that service—devoted... by the one in scrupulous, earnest, affectionate design; by the other in expenditure at least more frank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For revival of quality in art and architecture both designers and patrons must show genuine, uncalculating devotion: architects must design earnestly; employers/patrons must be more frank with expenditure than in private indulgence. The expected consequence is a national impulse and vitality in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do one's best; avoid half-work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is alone enough to secure success... neither architect nor builder has done his best... do not let us degrade ourselves voluntarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern work often looks like 'money's worth'—stopped short wherever possible. The rule is to put forth full strength: avoid half-worked rosettes, blunt details and lazy compliance. Better to leave parts unfinished than to complete them badly. This applies to design intent and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer good lower-order work to bad higher-order work
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer always what is good of a lower order of work or material, to what is bad of a higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one cannot afford high classical ornament, adopt a simpler style done to the highest standard possible (e.g., Norman hatchet work rather than poor Flaxman frieze; use Caen stone or the best brick available). Honest, well-executed simpler work is preferable to pretentious but poor high-style ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in continuation and termination of ornament (avoid deception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever, by the construction of a building, some parts of it are hidden from the eye which are the continuation of others bearing some consistent ornament, it is not well that the ornament should cease in the parts concealed; credit is given for it, and it should not be deceptively withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stop ornament deceptively where it becomes hidden; either carry ornament through or end it boldly with a distinct terminal motif. Example: sculptured backs of pediment statues should be finished even if rarely seen. The visual 'credit' given by continuity must not be cheated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute ornament according to visibility and distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep such as by their nature are delicate, down near the eye, and throwing the bold and rough kinds of work to the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ornament with the spectator's vantage in mind: delicate bas-reliefs and fine mouldings belong low and near the viewer; bold, coarse patterns belong higher and farther. Examples: San Zeno (bas-reliefs on lower front), Rouen transepts (delicate reliefs low, statues above), Florence campanile (reliefs low, statues above, mosaic/tracery higher). Avoid tiny, intricate work placed where it will be invisible or look like meaningless roughness from distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-delicate work unsuited to exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Work may be wasted by being too good for its material, or too fine to bear exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use extremely delicate ornament that cannot withstand weather and use (e.g., ivory-like incrustations that would be ruined by rain or frost). If ornament 'does its duty' and reads as decoration from a distance it may justify detail; otherwise it is false and pitiful. Choose durable forms appropriate to environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must serve the architectural purpose; good ornament is never 'overcharged'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament cannot be overcharged if it be good, and is always overcharged when it is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legitimacy of profuse ornament depends solely on its success as ornament—its ability to contribute to the general effect, speak at distance, and increase majesty/mystery. Good styles can bear luxuriance; simple styles owe part of their pleasure to contrast. Criticize ornament by its decorative power, not by quantity per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exhibitionary, surface, or tinsel decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment of the Papists' temple is eminently exhibitory; it is surface work throughout... its tinsel and glitter... in the gilding of the shrine and painting of the image... frequently thrust forward to the concealment of what is really good or great in their buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decoration should not be intended to win praise, show off wealth, or hide substantive qualities. Beware of surface glitter, embroidered dingy robes, imitated gems, and any decoration whose purpose is exhibition rather than devotion. Gifts to a church should be unpresuming; small, well-placed sacrifices (e.g., a porphyry shaft, extra labor on a capital) are preferable to ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness in craft and moral habit (Lamp of Truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The truthful practice of handicraftsmen... To speak and act truth with constancy and precision is nearly as difficult, and perhaps as meritorious, as to speak it under intimidation or penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond aesthetics, Ruskin demands moral truthfulness: avoid deception in speech and in workmanship (no faux finishes, graining, or dishonest effects). Cultivate the habit of truth in daily acts—this moral lamp supports the dignity of handicrafts. The 'Lamp of Truth' governs choice of materials, honest execution, and rejection of trickery in ornament and finish.
